title: Project: health checks and alerts
goal: Build a health-check tool: HTTP checks with timeouts and retries, disk and memory thresholds, clear exit codes, a log file, and alerts that do not spam.
setup: # a fake API for the checks (python3, only on 127.0.0.1)
import http.server, json, os, sys, time
# snapshots for the disk and memory checks

printf '%s\n' 'Filesystem     1024-blocks      Used Available Capacity Mounted on' '/dev/nvme0n1p1    51474912  47105112   4353416      92% /' '/dev/nvme1n1     103081248  41232499  56589645      43% /var' > df-p.txt

printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/bash' '# Runs every 5 minutes from cron. Appends ONE line per run to health.log.' '# Exit 0 if healthy, exit 2 if not (Nagios style). Must never wait longer than 3 seconds.' 'URL=${1:-http://127.0.0.1:8124/health}' 'if curl -s $URL > /dev/null; then' '  echo "$(date +%T) OK $URL" > health.log' 'else' '  echo "$(date +%T) DOWN $URL" > health.log' 'fi' > check-api.sh

warmup.q: Which curl options make a check fail on HTTP 500 and not hang?
warmup.a: `curl -fsS --max-time 5 URL` (`-f` fail on HTTP errors, `--max-time` limit).

warmup.q: How do you keep only the last 7 backups by name?
How do you read `df` output in a script reliably?
warmup.a: Use `df -P` (POSIX format), skip the header, and strip the `%`.

warmup.q: Which column of `/proc/meminfo` matters for free memory?

problems.title: An HTTP check with timeout and retries
problems.situation: The monitoring script calls the to-do API's `/health` endpoint. One slow or failed answer should not wake up the on-call engineer at night: the check retries a few times with a pause, and each try has a timeout.
task: Start the fake API: `python3 fake-api.py 8121 &`.
Write `check_url URL [tries] [delay]`: curl with `--max-time 2`, get the status code, accept only 2xx.
Print `OK` with the try number, or a `WARN` line per failed try (stderr), then `FAIL` and return 1.
Test `/health`, `/flaky` (fails twice, then works), `/health-db-down` (503), and `/slow` (too slow).
hints: A C-style loop: `for ((i = 1; i <= tries; i++))`.
solution: local url=$1 tries=${2:-3} delay=${3:-1} i code
if [[ $code == 2* ]]; then echo "OK   $url ($code, try $i)"; return 0; fi

explanation.meaning: Print only the status code (Day 18).
Give up after 2 seconds. A slow API counts as a failure.
When curl itself fails (timeout, refused), use `000`.
Pattern: any code that starts with 2 (Day 6).
Avoid false alarms from one short glitch.
The function answers yes/no; the caller decides what to do (Day 9).

problems.expected_output:
OK   http://127.0.0.1:8121/health (200, try 1)
WARN http://127.0.0.1:8121/flaky answered 500 (try 1/5)
WARN http://127.0.0.1:8121/flaky answered 500 (try 2/5)
OK   http://127.0.0.1:8121/flaky (200, try 3)
WARN http://127.0.0.1:8121/health-db-down answered 503 (try 1/2)
WARN http://127.0.0.1:8121/health-db-down answered 503 (try 2/2)
FAIL http://127.0.0.1:8121/health-db-down after 2 tries
exit code: 1
WARN http://127.0.0.1:8121/slow answered 000 (try 1/1)
FAIL http://127.0.0.1:8121/slow after 1 tries
exit code: 1
mistakes: Retrying without a pause: 3 tries in 10 ms are the same as 1 try.
Too many retries with long pauses: the check takes minutes and overlaps the next cron run. Keep total time below the schedule interval.
problems.interview_say: My HTTP check uses `curl` with a timeout and the status code, accepts only 2xx, retries a few times with a short pause, and returns 1 only after all tries fail, so one glitch does not page anyone.
problems.try_yourself: Also check the JSON body: `curl -s URL | grep -q '"status": "UP"'`. Why can a 200 answer still mean "not healthy"?

problems.title: Disk and memory thresholds you can test
problems.situation: The same tool must warn when a disk is above 90% or available memory is below 10%. To test the alert without filling a real disk, the functions read from files: `df -P` output on stdin, and a meminfo path in a variable that defaults to `/proc/meminfo`.
task: Write `check_disk LIMIT` that reads `df -P` lines from stdin and prints `ALERT disk MOUNT at N%` (return 1 if any).
Write `check_mem MIN_PCT` that reads `${MEMINFO:-/proc/meminfo}` and computes MemAvailable / MemTotal.
Test with `df-p.txt`, `meminfo-low.txt` and `meminfo-ok.txt`.
Run `check_mem 10` once on your real machine too.
hints: Reuse the df parsing from Day 17: skip the header, strip `%`.
`MEMINFO=meminfo-low.txt check_mem 10` sets the variable for one call only (Day 5).
solution: local limit=${1:-90} bad=0 fs size used avail pct mount
while read -r fs size used avail pct mount; do
if (( pct >= limit )); then echo "ALERT disk $mount at $pct% (limit $limit%)"; bad=1; fi
if (( pct < min )); then echo "ALERT memory available ${pct}% (minimum $min%)"; return 1; fi
check_disk 90 < df-p.txt; echo "disk check exit code: $?"
MEMINFO=meminfo-low.txt check_mem 10; echo "low memory exit code: $?"
MEMINFO=meminfo-ok.txt check_mem 10; echo "ok memory exit code: $?"
check_mem 10 > /dev/null && echo "this machine: memory OK" || echo "this machine: memory LOW"

explanation.meaning: `df -P | check_disk 90` in production, `< df-p.txt` in tests. Same code.
A default path that tests can change: easy testing without fake hardware.
Percent of RAM that new programs can still get.
0 = fine, 1 = at least one alert.
Integer comparison with normal operators (Day 6).

problems.expected_output:
ALERT disk / at 92% (limit 90%)
disk check exit code: 1
ALERT memory available 5% (minimum 10%)
low memory exit code: 1
OK   memory available 61%
ok memory exit code: 0
this machine: memory OK
problems.output_note: The last line depends on the user's machine (it is almost always OK on a laptop). The other lines are fixed.
mistakes: Alerting on `MemFree`: Linux keeps little memory free on purpose (cache), so the alert fires falsely every hour.
Testing alerts only in production. A threshold bug is found when the disk is already full.
problems.interview_say: My disk and memory checks read `df -P` and `/proc/meminfo`, compare with thresholds and return non-zero on alert. I make them read from stdin or a configurable path, so I can test the alert logic with saved files.
problems.try_yourself: Add an inode check: `df -Pi | check_disk 90`. Does the same function work?

problems.title: Log every run, alert only on change
problems.situation: The first version sent a Slack message every 5 minutes while the API was down: 100 messages in one night, so people muted the channel. Better: log every run, but alert only when the state changes (OK → DOWN, DOWN → OK). The last state is kept in a small state file.
task: Write `record STATE` that appends `time STATE` to `health.log`.
Keep the last state in `health.state`. If the new state is different, print `ALERT: STATE (was OLD)`.
Simulate 5 runs with states OK, DOWN, DOWN, DOWN, OK.
Show `health.log` and count the alerts.
hints: For tests, the time comes from `FAKE_NOW`: `date -d "${FAKE_NOW:-now}" '+%F %T'`.
solution: for state in OK DOWN DOWN DOWN OK; do
echo "alerts sent: $(wc -l < alerts.txt) (instead of 3 DOWN messages + 1 OK)"

explanation.meaning: Append: one line per run, the full history.
Remember the last state between cron runs.
One message when it breaks, one when it recovers. No spam.
Tests can set the time; in production it is empty and `date -d now` is used.
Show the alerts and save them (Day 4).

mistakes: Storing the state file in `/tmp`: after a reboot it is gone, and the first run may send a wrong "recovered" alert. Use `/var/lib/yourtool/`.
Alerting on the first failure only, with no recovery message: the team never knows when it is fixed.
problems.interview_say: To avoid alert fatigue I log every check, but send an alert only when the state changes, keeping the last state in a file. Real monitoring tools like Prometheus Alertmanager do the same with grouping and silences.
problems.try_yourself: Add a reminder: if the state is still DOWN after 6 runs (30 minutes), send one more alert.

problems.title: Find the bug: the cron health check
problems.situation: `check-api.sh` runs every 5 minutes. Last night the API returned 503 for an hour, but the script logged `OK`. The log file only ever has one line, and the monitoring server never saw a failure.
task: Start the fake API on 8124. Run `bash check-api.sh http://127.0.0.1:8124/health-db-down; echo $?` and read `health.log`.
Run it twice. How many lines are in `health.log`?
Find 4 bugs: no `-f`, no timeout, `>` instead of `>>`, and no exit code 2.
Fix it. Test `/health`, `/health-db-down` and `/slow`, and show the log without the time column.
hints: Without `-f`, curl's exit code is 0 for a 503 answer.
solution: echo "lines in health.log: $(wc -l < health.log)"; cut -d' ' -f2- health.log
# Runs every 5 minutes from cron. Appends ONE line per run to health.log.
# Exit 0 if healthy, exit 2 if not (Nagios style). Must never wait longer than 3 seconds.
for path in health health-db-down slow; do

explanation.meaning: Bug 1: the 503 page was a "successful" download, so the check said OK.
Bug 2: `/slow` would block the cron job for 5 seconds or more.
Bug 3: `>` replaced the log on every run, so the history was lost.
Bug 4: the script always ended with 0, so the monitoring server saw success.
Here only to hide the time column, which changes every run.

problems.expected_output:
exit code: 0
lines in health.log: 1
OK http://127.0.0.1:8124/health-db-down
--- fixed ---
health: exit code 0
health-db-down: exit code 2
slow: exit code 2
OK http://127.0.0.1:8124/health
DOWN http://127.0.0.1:8124/health-db-down
DOWN http://127.0.0.1:8124/slow
mistakes: Unquoted `$URL`: a URL with `&` in the query string breaks the command.
Running a health check from the same server as the app only. If the server is down, nothing alerts. Run checks from outside too.
problems.interview_say: A cron health check needs `curl -f` and a timeout, must append to its log, and must return a non-zero exit code on failure, so the scheduler or monitoring agent can react.
problems.try_yourself: Add a 1 (WARNING) exit code for answers slower than 1 second: use `-w '%{time_total}'`.

problems.title: Put it together: healthcheck.sh for cron
problems.situation: The final tool checks the API, the disks and the memory in one run, prints one summary line per check, writes everything to a log, returns Nagios-style exit codes (0 OK, 1 WARNING, 2 CRITICAL), and never overlaps itself.
task: Write `healthcheck.sh` with `set -uo pipefail` (not `-e`: a failed check must not stop the other checks).
Run 3 checks: API (critical if down), disk (warning above 90%), memory (warning below 10%).
Use `flock` so two runs never overlap. Append the summary to `healthcheck.log`.
Exit with the worst result. Test with good and bad inputs. Print the crontab line.
hints: Keep a variable `WORST=0`; after each check: `(( rc > WORST )) && WORST=$rc`.
solution: flock -n 9 || { echo "UNKNOWN: previous run still active"; exit 3; }
result() { echo "$1 $2"; echo "$(date '+%F %T') $1 $2" >> "$LOG"; (( $3 > WORST )) && WORST=$3; return 0; }
else result CRITICAL "api $URL is down" 2; fi
DISK=$({ [ -n "${DF_FILE:-}" ] && cat "$DF_FILE" || df -P; } | awk 'NR > 1 {gsub("%", "", $5); if ($5 >= 90) print $6 "=" $5 "%"}' | xargs)
if [ -z "$DISK" ]; then result OK "disk below 90%" 0; else result WARNING "disk $DISK" 1; fi
if (( MEM >= 10 )); then result OK "memory available $MEM%" 0; else result WARNING "memory available $MEM%" 1; fi
DF_FILE=/dev/null MEMINFO=meminfo-ok.txt bash healthcheck.sh; echo "exit code: $?"
echo "=== full disk and low memory ==="
DF_FILE=df-p.txt MEMINFO=meminfo-low.txt bash healthcheck.sh; echo "exit code: $?"
URL=http://127.0.0.1:8125/health-db-down DF_FILE=df-p.txt MEMINFO=meminfo-ok.txt bash healthcheck.sh; echo "exit code: $?"

explanation.meaning: A failing check is expected; the script must continue and report all checks.
No overlapping runs; 3 = UNKNOWN in Nagios style.
One place to print, log, and keep the worst code.
`URL`, `DF_FILE`, `MEMINFO`: real values by default, test files when set.
List all full mounts on one line, like `/=92%`.
0 OK, 1 WARNING, 2 CRITICAL: what Nagios, Icinga and many cron monitors expect.
Make it executable first: `chmod +x healthcheck.sh`.

=== all good ===
OK api http://127.0.0.1:8125/health
OK disk below 90%
OK memory available 61%
exit code: 0
=== full disk and low memory ===
OK api http://127.0.0.1:8125/health
WARNING disk /=92%
WARNING memory available 5%
exit code: 1
=== API down too ===
CRITICAL api http://127.0.0.1:8125/health-db-down is down
WARNING disk /=92%
OK memory available 61%
exit code: 2
log lines: 9
crontab: */5 * * * * cd /home/wicky/bash-practice/day25 && ./healthcheck.sh >> cron.out 2>&1
mistakes: Using `set -e` in a multi-check script: the first failed check stops everything, and the other results are never shown.
Mixing up exit codes: if both WARNING and CRITICAL happen, report CRITICAL (the worst).
problems.interview_say: My health check runs all checks even if one fails, logs each result, uses a lock to avoid overlapping runs, and exits with the worst status: 0 OK, 1 warning, 2 critical. Inputs come from environment variables so I can test the alert paths.
problems.try_yourself: Add a fourth check: the TLS certificate expiry of a site, with `openssl s_client` (needs internet). Warning when less than 14 days are left.

problems.title: Send the alert to a chat webhook (local test receiver)
problems.situation: Alerts go to the team's Slack or Teams channel through an incoming webhook: an HTTP POST with a small JSON body. Here a tiny local receiver plays Slack and saves what it gets, so nothing leaves the laptop.
task: Start the test receiver (see the solution, first lines). It saves each POST body into `received.json`.
Build the JSON safely with `printf` and proper quotes (or `jq -n` if installed).
POST it with `curl -fsS -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data "$PAYLOAD" URL`.
Show what the receiver got.
hints: The webhook URL is a secret: read it from a variable or file, never write it in the script.
`--data @file.json` sends a file as the body.
solution: PAYLOAD=$(printf '{"text": ":red_circle: CRITICAL on %s: api /health is down"}' "$HOST")

explanation.meaning: A secret URL; anything POSTed there appears in the channel.
Send JSON in the request body.
The body. Quote it, it contains spaces.
Real URL from the environment (a secret), test URL by default.
Fail on HTTP errors, quiet, but show errors (Day 18).

problems.expected_output:
ok
receiver got: {"text": ":red_circle: CRITICAL on todo-prod-1: api /health is down"}
mistakes: Putting user text into JSON without escaping: a `"` in the message breaks the JSON. Use `jq -n --arg t "$msg" '{text: $t}'`.
Committing the webhook URL to git: anyone can then post into the team channel. Keep it in a secret store or env file with 600 permissions (Day 26).
problems.interview_say: For chat alerts I POST a small JSON body to an incoming webhook with `curl -fsS`, build the JSON with jq to escape text safely, and keep the webhook URL as a secret, not in the code.
problems.try_yourself: If `jq` is installed: `jq -n --arg t 'He said "hi"' '{text: $t}'`. See how jq escapes the quotes.

interview.q: How would you write a simple health check for a web API?
interview.a: `curl -fsS --max-time 5 https://api/health`, check the status code (and maybe the JSON body), retry a few times with a pause, log the result, and exit non-zero on failure.

interview.q: What exit codes do monitoring tools like Nagios expect?
interview.a: 0 = OK, 1 = WARNING, 2 = CRITICAL, 3 = UNKNOWN. A check script should exit with the worst result.

interview.q: How do you avoid alert spam?
interview.a: Alert only when the state changes (keep the last state in a file), use retries for short glitches, and send a recovery message. Monitoring tools add grouping and silences.

interview.q: How do you test alert logic without breaking a real server?
interview.a: Make inputs configurable: read `df -P` from stdin, take the meminfo path and the URL from variables, and test with saved files and a fake API.

interview.q: Why should a health check have a timeout?
interview.a: A hanging service would make the check hang too. The check would then never report, and cron runs would pile up. A timeout turns "hanging" into a clear failure.

Remember the last state; alert on change
